blocks.text: Quick verdict

Infatica is the better value at small and mid volumes: $40 for 10 GB against $80 on Oxylabs PAYG, ZIP targeting on every plan, and a cheap seven-day trial that does not require a sales call. Oxylabs is the better choice for large, hard-target pipelines, where its pool is four to five times bigger, its published 99.95% success rate and Web Scraper API save engineering time, and its $2.50/GB Corporate rate beats Infatica's best published price. Both offer the sourcing paperwork compliance teams ask for.

Oxylabs and Infatica both lean heavily on ethical sourcing and compliance, which makes them natural candidates for procurement-sensitive buyers. They differ enormously in scale and price. Oxylabs advertises a 175M+ residential pool and sells a full enterprise stack of proxies and scraper APIs. Infatica advertises 35M-40M IPs, includes ZIP targeting on every plan and offers a $4 seven-day trial. This comparison shows when the enterprise option is worth the premium and when Infatica covers your needs for less.

blocks.text: Oxylabs in 2026: what you get

Oxylabs is a Lithuanian web-data company and Bright Data's closest rival at the top of the market. It advertises a residential pool of more than 175 million IPs across 195 locations, publishes a 99.95% success rate for residential traffic, and sells seven product lines including datacenter, ISP and mobile proxies, a Web Scraper API and Web Unblocker. Onboarding is more sales-led than the mid-market providers, but self-service has expanded through 2026, including dedicated ISP proxies.

Strengths: One of the two largest residential pools available; Published 99.95% residential success rate; Strong scraper APIs that bill per result; Formal ethical-sourcing documentation for procurement. Weak spots: Expensive at low volume ($8/GB PAYG); Best rates need large monthly commitments; Residential trial goes through sales rather than self-service.
Infatica in 2026: what you get

Infatica pitches itself on ethical sourcing and features available to every customer. All residential plans include country, city and ZIP targeting, IP whitelisting and selectable rotation times, and a 7-day $4 trial lowers the risk of testing. Independent reviewers have found its proxies fast and its pool modest but respectable. Its niche extra is a premium IPv6 residential pool, rare in this market, at about 1.5x the normal per-GB price.

Strengths: ZIP targeting included on every plan; Clear sourcing policy and ISO certifications; Cheap 7-day trial; Rare IPv6 residential pool. Weak spots: Mid-range pool size; Per-GB price stays above $3.50 until large volumes; Subscription traffic does not roll over.
Pricing: Oxylabs vs Infatica

Oxylabs charges $8/GB pay-as-you-go for residential traffic. Monthly plans start with Starter at $30 for 5 GB ($6/GB) and a Basic tier around $100 for 20 GB, and the rate falls to $2.50/GB on the $2,500/month Corporate plan. Mobile traffic starts at $7.50/GB.

Infatica charges $4/GB pay-as-you-go for residential traffic. Subscriptions cost $3.84/GB at 25 GB, $3.60/GB at 100 GB, and fall to about $2.70/GB at 500 GB and $2.60/GB at 1 TB. Premium IPv6 residential runs at roughly 1.5x those rates, starting at $6/GB.

For a 10 GB month, Infatica costs about $40 while Oxylabs costs about $80, so Infatica saves around 50%. At 100 GB, a like-for-like total is harder to state because Oxylabs does not publish an exact price for that volume; Infatica comes to about $360. Both Oxylabs and Infatica work on allowances that do not carry forward indefinitely, so size your plan to real monthly usage rather than buying ahead.
Pool size, coverage and targeting

Oxylabs has the bigger advertised network, 175M+ residential IPs against 35M-40M for Infatica, roughly 5.0 times larger. Advertised pool sizes are marketing figures counted over long periods; the number of IPs actually reachable in a given country at a given moment is far smaller for every provider, so treat these as a rough guide to depth rather than a guarantee. For coverage, Oxylabs lists 195 countries and Infatica lists 195. On targeting, Oxylabs offers country, state, city, ZIP and ASN, while Infatica offers country, state, city and ZIP.
Protocols, sessions and setup

Both providers support SOCKS5 as well as HTTP(S), so either will plug into scrapers, anti-detect browsers and automation tools that expect a SOCKS endpoint. On sessions, Oxylabs offers rotating and sticky sessions on residential and mobile, and Infatica offers per-request rotation or selectable rotation times. Both use a backconnect gateway: you point your tool at one host and port, and choose country, city or session behaviour through parameters in the username.
Which is better for your use case?

General web scraping: Oxylabs. Oxylabs has the edge here. Why: its pool size and Web Scraper API suit large crawls. How Infatica compares: fast proxies that did well on popular targets in independent tests.
SERP and rank tracking: Oxylabs wins. The deciding factor for Oxylabs: its scraper API returns parsed search results. The limitation on the Infatica side: ZIP targeting helps local search results.

Social media and multi-account management: tie. Neither has a clear edge. With Oxylabs: it works, but the pricing is built for volume, not a handful of accounts. With Infatica: rotation controls are good but very long sticky sessions are not a headline feature. Run the same small test on both before committing.

E-commerce price and stock monitoring: Oxylabs wins. The deciding factor for Oxylabs: city and ZIP targeting plus parsed e-commerce endpoints. The limitation on the Infatica side: ZIP-level targeting for local prices.

Ad verification and geo-testing: tie. Neither has a clear edge. With Oxylabs: broad geo coverage with ASN targeting. With Infatica: precise geo targeting and clean sourcing. Run the same small test on both before committing.
Tight budgets: Infatica. Infatica has the edge here. Why: mid-range pricing until you reach large volumes. How Oxylabs compares: entry pricing is among the highest in this comparison.
Trials, verification and billing fine print

Before you pay, check how each provider lets you test. Oxylabs: Residential trial arranged through sales, once per customer. Infatica: 7-day trial for $4 (residential) or $8 (mobile). Verification and payment rules differ too. Oxylabs: Business verification on larger accounts. Infatica: Standard verification; states it does not resell IPs. Whichever you choose, measure cost per successful request rather than cost per gigabyte: retries, blocked pages and heavy page assets all burn bandwidth, and a cheaper network that fails more often can end up costing more. Blocking images and fonts in your scraper, reusing sessions where a target allows it, and capping concurrency are the quickest ways to cut the bill on either provider.
How to test Oxylabs and Infatica before you commit
The quickest way to choose between Oxylabs and Infatica is a side-by-side test on the sites and countries you actually care about:
1. Buy the smallest option on each side (Oxylabs: residential trial arranged through sales, once per customer; Infatica: 7-day trial for $4 (residential) or $8 (mobile)).
2. Pick three to five real target URLs and the two or three countries that matter most, and send the same number of requests (a few hundred is enough) through each provider at the same time of day.
3. Record success rate, median response time, CAPTCHAs or blocks, and the number of unique exit IPs you received per country.
4. Divide what you spent by the number of successful, correctly located responses to get cost per useful request, then scale that to your monthly volume.
Bottom line

Across the six use cases above, Oxylabs comes out ahead in 3, Infatica in 1, and 2 are ties. That makes Oxylabs the safer default if you are unsure, but the right answer still depends on your volume and targets: Oxylabs is strongest for large scraping pipelines with steady volume, while Infatica is strongest for compliance-conscious buyers. If you can, spend a few dollars testing both on the exact sites and countries you care about; a one-hour test tells you more than any spec sheet.
